blogs.title: Digital Delivery vs. Physical Possession: The Fifth Circuit Modernizes 'Receipt' in Insurance Cancellations
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Fifth Circuit's pivotal interpretation of the term "receipt" under La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550. While Louisiana courts traditionally demand "strict adherence" to statutory cancellation procedures, the *Williams* decision validates a fully automated workflow where an insurer's computer system processes an email request and executes cancellation before any human intervention occurs. The analysis explores how the court reconciled traditional concepts of "taking physical possession" with modern web services and API interactions, signaling a shift toward recognizing digital automation as legally equivalent to manual receipt in regulatory contexts.

blogs.title: The Signature Dilemma: Can a Corporation Certify Without a Human Hand?
blogs.description: Focusing on the procedural nuance of corporate certification, this article examines the plaintiffs' argument that a premium finance company's notice of cancellation is invalid without a specific employee's signature prior to the effective date of cancellation. The Fifth Circuit rejected this formalistic requirement, reasoning that the statute empowers the "company" to certify rather than a specific individual. This post discusses the tension between strict statutory construction and practical business realities, questioning whether the absence of a pre-cancellation signature undermines the reliability of mass-market insurance administration or merely reflects an outdated view of corporate agency.

blogs.title: Declining to Certify: Why Federal Courts Hesitate to Ask State Supreme Courts for Help
blogs.description: Beyond the substantive insurance law, *Williams v. GoAuto* offers a fascinating look at federal-state judicial comity through its refusal to certify questions to the Louisiana Supreme Court. Despite acknowledging that no Louisiana precedent explicitly addressed whether an unsigned notice constitutes valid certification or defining "receipt" in an era of automated systems, Judge Southwick declined certification based on established Fifth Circuit precedent discouraging frequent referrals unless absolutely necessary. This piece evaluates the strategic calculus behind declining certification and speculates on how this creates binding federal interpretations of state statutes that may diverge from future state court rulings.
